paragraphs.text: Lesson 28, wealth and poverty.
Two friends, Janet and Elise, discussed the political views of Elise's husband.
Listen to their conversation and mark the statements true or false.
I can't believe your husband is a Republican.
Didn't you know that when you tied the knot?
When we were dating, he was always pretty tight-lipped about his political views.
He described himself as a moderate.
And whenever he brought up points that countered my opinions,
I figured he was just playing devil's advocate.
He misled you though.
I mean, every relationship has its ups and downs,
but that's a serious breach of trust.
Don't tell me you're going to stick with him.
Look, some of his comments do rub me the wrong way,
but it's not like we're at each other's throats about these issues.
You've got to pick your battles, and I'm not about to end my marriage
just because we don't see eye to eye on some things.
But doesn't it make you think less of his character?
Republicans are selfish and stingy.
How can you make a blanket statement like that?
You know Michael. He's a kind and generous man.
Just look at the Republican stance on economics, for instance.
They favor the rich and think the poor should pull themselves up by their bootstraps.
I don't think it's quite that simple.
Granted, I don't eat, sleep, and breathe politics like you do, but...
Let me break it down for you.
Republicans want tax breaks for the wealthy.
The rationale is that rich people will spend more money and stimulate the economy for everybody.
But the distribution of wealth in this country is already so lopsided.
How can anyone argue that helping the rich stay rich will solve the problem?
We do our part, though. We donate to charity.
And I've never heard Michael make a disparaging remark about poor people.
Economics aren't my strong suit, but I'm pretty sure he's not rooting for people to starve just so we can get a tax break.
But people are starving.
Just look at the number of destitute families in our soup kitchen every week.
In my line of work, we have to fight tooth and nail against Republican policy.
They're always the ones shutting down social programs, saying that people shouldn't be getting handouts.
Republicans want to keep their privileged position while looking down on everyone else who isn't so fortunate.
Hey, Michael may be a Republican, but you can't make him out to be some sort of villain.
I've pretty much come to terms with the fact that he may just have different ideas about how to accomplish the same goals.
He cares about helping people. He just doesn't believe in squandering resources on government programs with bloated bureaucracies, as he puts it.
You're delusional if you think Republicans actually want poor people to go hungry.
Sometimes it seems that way.
And sometimes you sound like a broken record.
Oh, look at the time. I better get going.
Let's learn the vocabulary from this dialogue.
Janna is surprised that Elise didn't know about her husband's political views when she tied the knot.
Tied the knot is an informal expression for got married.
Elise says that when she and her husband were dating, he was pretty tight-lipped about his political views.
Tight-lipped means reluctant to speak. He kept his mouth closed about his political views.
Sometimes, though, he brought up points that countered Elise's opinions, but Elise figured he was just playing devil's advocate.
Playing devil's advocate means arguing from the opposite point of view just to generate some discussion.
If you play devil's advocate, you don't really believe the other side, but you bring up their point simply to help the conversation develop.
Janet says that Elise's husband misled her.
To mislead somebody means to influence the person to believe something that isn't true.
Every relationship has its ups and downs.
Ups and downs are good times and bad times.
But Janet says, that's a serious breach of trust.
A breach means a break, especially of an agreement.
Then Janet says, don't tell me you're going to stick with him.
Stick with him means stay with him. Stay married to him in this case.
Elise admits that some of her husband's comments do rub her the wrong way.
If something rubs you the wrong way, it means it irritates or annoys you a little bit.
But she says that they're not at each other's throats about these issues.
If two people are at each other's throats, it means that they are in a very angry disagreement.
Elise says, you've got to pick your battles.
To pick your battles means to choose which things you are willing to fight for
and which things you are willing to tolerate or let go.
She says, I'm not about to end my marriage just because we don't see eye to eye on some things.
Don't see eye to eye means don't agree.
Don't have the same point of view.
Janet asks Elise if her husband's political views make her think less of his character,
because, according to her, Republicans are selfish and stingy.
Stingy is the opposite of generous.
A stingy person is not willing to give to help others.
Elise can't believe that Janet has made a blanket statement like that.
To make a blanket statement means to generalize, to make a general statement about an entire group of people,
as if they were all the same.
She says that her husband Michael is a kind and generous man.
Janet then talks about the Republican's stance on economics.
Stance means position or opinion.
Janet says that Republicans favor the rich.
Favor, as a verb, means to prefer or to provide preferential treatment to.
And Republicans think the poor should just pull themselves up by their bootstraps.
This expression, pull themselves up by their bootstraps, means to improve their situation
by their own effort, without assistance.
Elise doesn't think it's quite that simple, although she says,
I don't eat, sleep, and breathe politics like you do.
If you eat, sleep, and breathe a particular topic or activity, it means you're constantly
thinking about and working with it.
Janet offers to break it down for Elise.
To break it down means to explain something and make it simple.
Republicans want tax breaks for the wealthy.
The rationale is that rich people will spend more money and stimulate the economy for everybody.
Rational means reasoning or a logical sequence of thought.
But Janet claims that the distribution of wealth in this country is already so lopsided.
To be lopsided means to be unequal, to have more on one side than the other.
But Elise says that she's never heard Michael make a disparaging remark about poor people.
Disparaging means insulting and disrespectful.
Elise says that economics aren't her strong suit.
If something isn't your strong suit, it means it's not an area in which you're skilled or knowledgeable.
But she's pretty sure her husband is not rooting for people to starve.
If you're rooting for something, it means you're hoping for and wanting it to happen.
And starve means to suffer and die from lack of food.
Janet says that people are starving.
Just look at the number of destitute families in our soup kitchen every week.
Destitute means poor, completely lacking resources for survival.
And a soup kitchen is a center where food is served free to poor people.
In Janet's line of work, she has to fight tooth and nail against Republican policy.
To fight tooth and nail means to fight very intensely, using all possible resources.
According to Janet, Republicans don't want people to get handouts.
Handouts are things given for free.
Elise defends her husband.
She says Michael may be a Republican, but you can't make him out to be some sort of villain.
Make him out to be means describe him in a certain way.
And a villain is an evil person.
Elise has pretty much come to terms with the fact that he may just have different ideas.
If you come to terms with something, it means you learn to accept and tolerate it over time.
Michael just doesn't believe in squandering resources.
Squandering means wasting.
Especially wasting resources on government programs with bloated bureaucracies.
The word bloated means much bigger than it should be, so in Michael's opinion,
government bureaucracy is much larger than it should be.
Elise finishes this sentence by saying, as he puts it.
As he puts it means expressing this idea using the words that he uses.
In other words, Elise just use Michael's words to express this idea.
Then she says Janet is delusional, she thinks Republicans actually want poor people to go hungry.
Delusional means crazy, holding a completely false belief that is in no way based on reality.
Finally, Elise says that Janet sometimes sounds like a broken record.
If someone sounds like a broken record, it means that person keeps saying the same things repeatedly.
Finally, Elise sees what time it is and says she has to go.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
